reminder: A phase space has one point for each complete state of a classical system.
definition: The phase space of a classical system is the [space](c:space) whose points are the complete states of the system. In Hamiltonian mechanics a state is a position together with a momentum, and the phase space is a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold), often a [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle). In the covariant form, a point is a whole solution of the equations of motion.
examples: A free particle on a line has phase space $\mathbb{R}^2$ with coordinates $(q,p)$.
A pendulum has phase space $S^1\times\mathbb{R}$: an angle and an angular momentum.
For a harmonic oscillator, each orbit of the motion is an ellipse around the origin of the $(q,p)$ plane.
Non-example: the [configuration space](c:configuration-space-physics) alone, with positions only, is not a phase space, because a position does not fix the future motion.

steps: Take a Hamiltonian system with configuration space $Q$.
Its phase space is the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle) $T^*Q$ with coordinates $(q,p)$.
The form $\omega=\sum_i dq_i\wedge dp_i$ is closed and non-degenerate, so $T^*Q$ is a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold).
The physical case adds a Hamiltonian function that generates the motion.
links.why: It shows that every result about symplectic manifolds also holds for a Hamiltonian phase space.

reminder: The number $\pi$ is the circumference of a [circle](c:circle) divided by its diameter.
definition: The number $\pi\approx3.14159$ is the [real number](c:real-number) that equals the circumference of a [circle](c:circle) divided by its diameter, and this ratio is the same for every circle. Equivalently, $\pi$ is the length of half of the unit circle, so $2\pi$ is the length of the whole unit circle.
examples: A circle of radius $r$ has circumference $2\pi r$ and area $\pi r^2$.
The values $\sin\pi=0$ and $e^{i\pi}=-1$ both involve $\pi$.
Non-example: the fraction $22/7$ is only an approximation of $\pi$. The number $\pi$ is irrational, so no fraction equals it.

reminder: A planar [vector field](c:vector-field) gives each point of a region of the plane one vector.
definition: A planar vector field on an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$ is a map $F:U\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $F(x,y)=(P(x,y),Q(x,y))$, that attaches the vector $F(x,y)$ to the point $(x,y)$. It is usually continuously differentiable, so that the system $\dot x=P(x,y)$, $\dot y=Q(x,y)$ has unique solutions.
examples: The field $F(x,y)=(-y,x)$ turns every point around the origin, and its solution curves are circles.
The field $F(x,y)=(x,y)$ points away from the origin, and its solution curves are rays.
The gradient $(\partial_xf,\partial_yf)$ of a smooth function $f(x,y)$ is a planar vector field.
Non-example: a function $f(x,y)$ with real values is a scalar field, not a vector field, because it attaches a number and not a vector to each point.

steps: Take a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and its [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle).
A vector field on $M$ is a section of the tangent bundle.
Let $M$ be an open subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, so the tangent space at each point is $\mathbb{R}^2$.
A section is then a pair of functions $(P,Q)$, which is a planar vector field.
links.why: It shows that general facts about vector fields, such as flows and Lie brackets, hold for planar fields.

reminder: The plurigenus $P_m$ counts the independent global sections of the $m$-th power of the [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle).
definition: For a smooth [projective variety](c:projective-variety) $X$ with [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) $K_X$, the $m$-th plurigenus is $P_m(X)=\dim H^0(X,K_X^{\otimes m})$, the dimension of the space of global [sections](c:section) of the $m$-th tensor power of $K_X$. It is a birational invariant of $X$, and $P_1(X)$ is the geometric genus.
examples: For projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$ one has $P_m=0$ for every $m\ge1$, because $K^{\otimes m}=\mathcal{O}(-m(n+1))$ has no non-zero global section.
For an elliptic curve the canonical bundle is trivial, so $P_m=1$ for every $m\ge0$.
For a smooth curve of genus $g\ge2$, the Riemann-Roch theorem gives $P_m=(2m-1)(g-1)$ for $m\ge2$.
Non-example: $\dim H^0(\mathbb{P}^n,\mathcal{O}(1))=n+1$ is not a plurigenus, because $\mathcal{O}(1)$ is not a power of the canonical bundle.

reminder: The Poincaré [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) is the Lie algebra of the isometries of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space).
definition: The Poincaré Lie algebra $\mathfrak{iso}(\mathbb{R}^{d-1,1})$ is the [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) of the [Poincaré group](c:poincare-group), the group of isometries of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space). It is the [semidirect product](c:semidirect-product-lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{so}(d-1,1)\ltimes\mathbb{R}^d$ of the Lorentz Lie algebra with the abelian Lie algebra of translations, so it has dimension $d(d+1)/2$.
examples: For $d=4$ it has dimension $10$: six Lorentz generators (three rotations and three boosts) and four translations.
The translations $P_\mu$ commute with each other, $[P_\mu,P_\nu]=0$, while a Lorentz generator $M_{\mu\nu}$ turns the translations into each other.
Non-example: the Lorentz Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(d-1,1)$ alone is not the Poincaré Lie algebra, because it has no translations.

steps: Take the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{so}(d-1,1)$ and its defining action on $V=\mathbb{R}^d$.
Give $V$ the zero bracket, so it is an abelian Lie algebra on which $\mathfrak{g}$ acts by derivations.
The semidirect product $\mathfrak{g}\ltimes V$ has the bracket $[(A,v),(B,w)]=([A,B],Aw-Bv)$.
For these choices $\mathfrak{g}\ltimes V$ is the Poincaré Lie algebra.
links.why: It shows how the Lorentz part and the translations fit together in one bracket.

steps: The Poincaré Lie algebra is a real vector space with a bilinear bracket.
The bracket is antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity, because it comes from the Lie group of isometries.
So the space with this bracket is a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra).
The special case adds the splitting into Lorentz generators and translations.
links.why: It shows what the Poincaré case adds to a Lie algebra: the Lorentz and translation parts.

reminder: The Poincaré [line bundle](c:line-bundle) is the universal family of degree-zero line bundles on an abelian variety.
definition: Let $A$ be an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) and $A^\vee=\mathrm{Pic}^0(A)$ its dual, a component of the [Picard scheme](c:picard-scheme). The Poincaré line bundle $\mathcal{P}$ on $A\times A^\vee$ restricts on each slice $A\times\{\xi\}$ to the line bundle $L_\xi$ that the point $\xi$ represents, and it is trivial on $\{0\}\times A^\vee$.
examples: For an elliptic curve $E$ with origin $e$, identify $E\cong E^\vee$ by $p\mapsto\mathcal{O}(p-e)$. Then $\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{O}(\Delta-\{e\}\times E-E\times\{e\})$, where $\Delta$ is the diagonal.
The restriction of $\mathcal{P}$ to $A\times\{0\}$ is the trivial bundle, because the point $0\in A^\vee$ represents the trivial bundle.
Non-example: the trivial bundle on $A\times A^\vee$ restricts trivially to every slice $A\times\{\xi\}$, so it misses the non-trivial elements of $\mathrm{Pic}^0(A)$.

reminder: A point of a [topos](c:topos) is a [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) from the topos of sets into it.
definition: A point of a [topos](c:topos) $E$ is a [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) $x:\mathbf{Set}\to E$ from the topos of [sets](c:set). Its inverse image $x^*:E\to\mathbf{Set}$ preserves finite limits and colimits, and for a topos of sheaves on a space it sends a sheaf to its [stalk](c:stalk) at the point.
examples: For a [sober space](c:sober-topological-space) $X$, the points of the topos of sheaves $\mathrm{Sh}(X)$ are exactly the points of $X$.
For a small category $C$, the points of the presheaf topos $[C^{op},\mathbf{Set}]$ are the [flat functors](c:flat-functor) $C\to\mathbf{Set}$.
Non-example: for a complete atomless Boolean algebra $B$, seen as a [locale](c:locale), the topos of sheaves has no point, because a point would be a completely prime filter of $B$ and there is none.

steps: Start with a [geometric morphism](c:geometric-morphism) $f:F\to E$, which is an adjoint pair $f^*\dashv f_*$ with $f^*$ preserving finite limits.
Add the condition that the domain $F$ is the topos $\mathbf{Set}$ of sets.
The adjoint pair is then a pair of functors between $E$ and sets, and $f^*$ is a fibre functor.
This geometric morphism is a point of $E$.
links.why: It shows that a point is a geometric morphism out of the simplest topos, so results on geometric morphisms apply.

reminder: The Poisson bracket of two functions is antisymmetric, bilinear, obeys the Jacobi identity and the Leibniz rule.
definition: A Poisson bracket is a bilinear operation $\{\cdot,\cdot\}$ on [smooth functions](c:smooth-function) that is antisymmetric, satisfies the Jacobi identity and obeys the Leibniz rule $\{f,gh\}=\{f,g\}h+g\{f,h\}$. On a [symplectic manifold](c:symplectic-manifold) it comes from the symplectic form, and in canonical coordinates $\{f,g\}=\sum_i(\partial_{q_i}f\,\partial_{p_i}g-\partial_{p_i}f\,\partial_{q_i}g)$.
examples: For canonical coordinates, $\{q_i,p_j\}=\delta_{ij}$ and $\{q_i,q_j\}=\{p_i,p_j\}=0$.
For the angular momentum components $L_x=yp_z-zp_y$ and $L_y=zp_x-xp_z$, one gets $\{L_x,L_y\}=L_z$.
For a Hamiltonian $H$, a function $f$ changes along the motion at the rate $\dot f=\{f,H\}$.
Non-example: the pointwise product $(f,g)\mapsto fg$ is bilinear but symmetric, so it is not a Poisson bracket, which must be antisymmetric.

steps: Take the vector space of smooth functions on a symplectic manifold.
The Poisson bracket is bilinear and antisymmetric.
It satisfies the Jacobi identity, so these functions with this bracket form a Lie algebra, and the bracket is a [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket).
The special case adds the Leibniz rule, so each map $\{f,\cdot\}$ is a derivation of the product.
links.why: It shows that smooth functions form a Lie algebra whose bracket also respects the product.

reminder: A Poisson process counts random events that occur at a constant average rate, independently of each other.
definition: A Poisson process with rate $\lambda>0$ is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(N_t)_{t\ge0}$ with $N_0=0$ and [independent increments](c:independent-increments), such that $N_t-N_s$ has the [Poisson distribution](c:poisson-distribution) with mean $\lambda(t-s)$ for $s<t$. Its paths are right-continuous step functions that jump by $1$, and the times between jumps are independent exponential random variables with mean $1/\lambda$.
examples: The number of calls that reach a telephone exchange by time $t$ is modelled by a Poisson process when calls come independently at a constant average rate.
The decays of a large sample of a radioactive element, counted over time, follow a Poisson process to a good approximation.
The gaps $T_1,T_2-T_1,T_3-T_2,\dots$ between the arrival times of a Poisson process are independent with mean $1/\lambda$.
Non-example: a clock that ticks exactly once per second is not a Poisson process, because its gaps are constant and its increments are not Poisson.

reminder: A pole is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) where the absolute value of the function grows without bound.
definition: A pole of a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) $f$ is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) $z_0$ at which $|f(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to z_0$. Equivalently, $f(z)=g(z)/(z-z_0)^n$ near $z_0$, where $g$ is holomorphic with $g(z_0)\neq0$ and the integer $n\ge1$ is the order of the pole.
examples: The function $1/z$ has a simple pole at $0$, and $1/(z^2-1)$ has simple poles at $1$ and $-1$.
The function $1/z^3$ has a pole of order $3$ at $0$, and $\tan z$ has a simple pole at each point $\pi/2+k\pi$.
Non-example: $\sin(z)/z$ has a removable singularity at $0$, and $e^{1/z}$ has an [essential singularity](c:essential-singularity) at $0$, so neither is a pole.

steps: A pole $z_0$ of $f$ has a punctured disc around it on which $f$ is holomorphic.
So $z_0$ is an [isolated singularity](c:isolated-singularity) of $f$.
The [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) of $f$ at $z_0$ has a principal part, the terms with negative powers.
The singularity is a pole exactly when the principal part has finitely many terms and at least one.
links.why: It sorts isolated singularities into removable ones, poles and essential ones by the principal part.

reminder: A triangulation of a [polygon](c:polygon) cuts it into [triangles](c:triangle) by diagonals that do not cross.
definition: A triangulation of a [simple polygon](c:simple-polygon) is a set of non-crossing diagonals that cut the polygon into [triangles](c:triangle), so that every vertex of every triangle is a vertex of the polygon. A simple polygon with $n$ vertices always has a triangulation, and every triangulation has $n-3$ diagonals and $n-2$ triangles.
examples: A convex quadrilateral has two triangulations, one for each diagonal.
A convex hexagon cut by the three diagonals from one vertex gives four triangles.
A convex $n$-gon has $C_{n-2}$ triangulations, where $C_k$ is the $k$-th Catalan number.
Non-example: the two diagonals of a convex quadrilateral together cross, so they do not form a triangulation.

steps: Take the region that the polygon bounds, as a topological space.
The triangles of the polygon triangulation, with their edges and vertices, form a 2-dimensional simplicial complex.
The triangles meet only along common edges or vertices, so the geometric realization of this complex is the union of the triangles.
That union is the polygon region, so the complex is a [triangulation](c:triangulation) of the region.
links.why: It shows that polygon triangulation is the plane case of triangulating a topological space.

reminder: A polygonal number counts the dots in a growing pattern of regular polygons with a common corner.
definition: For $s\ge3$, the $n$-th $s$-gonal number is $P(s,n)=\frac{(s-2)n^2-(s-4)n}{2}$, the sum of the first $n$ terms $1,\,1+(s-2),\,1+2(s-2),\dots$ of an arithmetic progression. It counts the dots in $n$ nested regular $s$-gons that share a corner, where the sides have $1,2,\dots,n$ dots.
examples: The triangular numbers ($s=3$) are $1,3,6,10$, the square numbers ($s=4$) are $1,4,9,16$, and the pentagonal numbers ($s=5$) are $1,5,12,22$.
For $s=6$, $P(6,n)=n(2n-1)$ gives the hexagonal numbers $1,6,15,28$.
Non-example: $8$ is not a triangular number, because the triangular numbers jump from $6$ to $10$.

steps: Start with the formula $P(s,n)=((s-2)n^2-(s-4)n)/2$ for the $s$-gonal numbers.
These numbers are the sums $1+2+\dots+n$.
So the $3$-gonal numbers are exactly the [triangular numbers](c:triangular-number).
links.why: It shows that the triangular numbers are the case of three sides in a family of polygonal numbers.

reminder: A polynomial automorphism is an invertible map of affine space, given by polynomials, whose inverse is also given by polynomials.
definition: A polynomial automorphism of $K^n$ is a map $F=(F_1,\dots,F_n):K^n\to K^n$ whose components are [polynomials](c:polynomial) in $x_1,\dots,x_n$, such that a polynomial map $G$ exists with $G\circ F=F\circ G=\mathrm{id}$. Equivalently, $F$ gives a $K$-algebra [automorphism](c:automorphism) $g\mapsto g\circ F$ of the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $K[x_1,\dots,x_n]$.
examples: Every invertible affine map $x\mapsto Ax+b$ is a polynomial automorphism of $K^n$.
The shear $(x,y)\mapsto(x+y^2,y)$ is a polynomial automorphism with inverse $(x,y)\mapsto(x-y^2,y)$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is a bijection, but its inverse $x\mapsto x^{1/3}$ is not a polynomial.

steps: A polynomial automorphism $F$ is an invertible morphism from [affine space](c:affine-space) $K^n$ to itself, where morphisms are polynomial maps.
An invertible morphism from an object to itself is an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of that object.
So $F$ is an automorphism of $K^n$ in the category of affine varieties.
The special case is the object $K^n$ with morphisms given by polynomials.
links.why: It shows that polynomial automorphisms form a group under composition, the automorphism group of affine space.

reminder: Division of a polynomial $f$ by a non-zero polynomial $g$ gives a unique quotient $q$ and a remainder $r$ of smaller degree.
definition: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field), and let $f,g$ be [polynomials](c:polynomial) over $K$ with $g\neq0$. There are unique polynomials $q$ and $r$ with $f=qg+r$ and either $r=0$ or $\deg r<\deg g$, where $\deg$ is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-polynomial). Long division finds them by removing the leading term of what is left, one step at a time.
examples: Dividing $x^3-1$ by $x-1$ gives quotient $x^2+x+1$ and remainder $0$.
Dividing $x^2+1$ by $x-2$ gives quotient $x+2$ and remainder $5$, which is the value of $x^2+1$ at $2$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ one cannot divide $x$ by $2x$ with a remainder of smaller degree, because the leading coefficient $2$ has no inverse in $\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take the ring $K[x]$ of polynomials over a field, with the function $d(f)=\deg f$ on non-zero polynomials.
Polynomial division gives $f=qg+r$ with $r=0$ or $d(r)<d(g)$.
This is exactly the division with remainder that defines a Euclidean function.
So $K[x]$ is a [Euclidean domain](c:euclidean-domain), and polynomial division is its division with remainder.
links.why: It shows that the Euclidean algorithm and unique factorization work for polynomials over a field.

reminder: The order dimension of a poset is the least number of total orders whose intersection is the given order.
definition: The order dimension of a [partially ordered set](c:partial-order) $(P,\le)$ is the smallest $d$ such that $\le$ is the intersection of $d$ [total orders](c:total-order) on $P$. Equivalently, it is the smallest $d$ for which $P$ embeds in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the [product order](c:product-order).
examples: A chain has dimension $1$, because its order is already total.
An antichain with at least two elements has dimension $2$: take one total order and its reverse.
For $n\ge2$, the standard example with elements $a_1,\dots,a_n,b_1,\dots,b_n$ and $a_i<b_j$ exactly when $i\neq j$ has dimension $n$.
Non-example: the dimension is not the width. An antichain with $n$ elements has width $n$ but dimension $2$ when $n\ge2$.

reminder: A positive definite kernel is a symmetric function whose matrices on finite sets of points are positive semidefinite.
definition: A positive definite kernel on a set $X$ is a [symmetric function](c:symmetric-function) $K:X\times X\to\mathbb{R}$ such that $\sum_{i,j=1}^nc_ic_jK(x_i,x_j)\ge0$ for all points $x_1,\dots,x_n\in X$ and all real numbers $c_1,\dots,c_n$. Equivalently, every matrix $(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Such a kernel is the reproducing kernel of exactly one [reproducing kernel Hilbert space](c:rkhs) of functions on $X$.
examples: The Gaussian kernel $K(x,y)=e^{-|x-y|^2/2}$ and the linear kernel $K(x,y)=\langle x,y\rangle$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ are positive definite.
On $[0,\infty)$ the kernel $K(x,y)=\min(x,y)$ is positive definite, because it is the covariance of Brownian motion.
Non-example: $K(x,y)=|x-y|$ is symmetric but not positive definite, because the points $0$ and $1$ give the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which has the eigenvalue $-1$.

steps: Take a real symmetric [positive semidefinite matrix](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix) $M$ of size $n\times n$.
Let $X=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and define $K(i,j)=M_{ij}$.
Then $K$ is symmetric, and $\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(i,j)=c^TMc\ge0$ for every real vector $c$.
So $K$ is a positive definite kernel on $X$, and kernels on larger sets extend this case.
links.why: It shows that a kernel is a positive semidefinite matrix whose rows and columns are indexed by any set.

reminder: A positive-definite kernel on an interval is a continuous symmetric function whose integral operator is positive.
definition: A positive-definite kernel on a compact interval $[a,b]$ is a continuous symmetric function $K:[a,b]^2\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\int_a^b\int_a^bK(x,y)f(x)f(y)\,dx\,dy\ge0$ for every square-integrable function $f$. Equivalently, every matrix $(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j}$ is [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix), and the integral operator $f\mapsto\int_a^bK(\cdot,y)f(y)\,dy$ has only non-negative [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue).
examples: The kernel $K(x,y)=\cos(x-y)=\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y$ on $[0,2\pi]$ is positive-definite, because the double integral equals $(\int f\cos)^2+(\int f\sin)^2$.
The kernel $K(x,y)=\min(x,y)$ on $[0,1]$ is positive-definite, and its eigenvalues are $1/((k-\tfrac12)\pi)^2$ for $k=1,2,\dots$.
Non-example: the constant kernel $K(x,y)=-1$ is continuous and symmetric, but the choice $f=1$ gives the double integral $-(b-a)^2<0$.

steps: Let $K$ be a continuous symmetric kernel on $[a,b]$ with $\iint K(x,y)f(x)f(y)\,dx\,dy\ge0$ for all square-integrable $f$.
Fix points $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and real numbers $c_1,\dots,c_n$, and choose narrow bumps $f_\varepsilon$ of mass $c_i$ around each $x_i$.
Since $K$ is continuous, $\iint K f_\varepsilon f_\varepsilon\to\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(x_i,x_j)$ as the bumps shrink.
Each of these double integrals is non-negative, so the limit $\sum c_ic_jK(x_i,x_j)\ge0$, and $K$ is a [positive definite kernel](c:positive-definite-kernel).
links.why: It shows that the integral condition on an interval implies the pointwise condition on finite sets of points.

reminder: The power $a^n$ is the product of $n$ copies of $a$, and it extends to other exponents by fixed rules.
definition: For a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$, the power $a^n$ is the product of $n$ copies of $a$ under [multiplication](c:multiplication), with $a^0=1$. It extends to integer exponents by $a^{-n}=1/a^n$ for $a\neq0$, and to [real number](c:real-number) exponents by $a^x=e^{x\ln a}$ for $a>0$, using the [exponential function](c:exponential-function). In all cases $a^{x+y}=a^xa^y$.
examples: For every $a>0$ one has $a^{x+y}=a^xa^y$, for example $2^3\cdot2^2=2^5$.
Non-example: $0^{-1}$ is not defined, because $0$ has no inverse.

steps: Start with the power function $x\mapsto a^x$ for a base $a>0$.
Choose the base $a=e$.
Then $a^x=e^{x\ln e}=e^x$, which is the [exponential function](c:exponential-function).
Every other base satisfies $a^x=\exp(x\ln a)$, so the exponential function gives all powers.
links.why: It shows that every power function is the exponential function after a change of scale in the exponent.

reminder: A presentable $(\infty,1)$-category has all small colimits and is generated by a small set of compact objects under filtered colimits.
definition: An $(\infty,1)$-category $C$ is presentable when it is locally small, has all small [colimits](c:colimit), and is $\kappa$-accessible for some [regular cardinal](c:is-regular) $\kappa$: a small set of $\kappa$-[compact objects](c:compact-object) generates $C$ under $\kappa$-filtered colimits. Equivalently, $C$ is a reflective subcategory of a [presheaf](c:presheaf) $(\infty,1)$-category on a small one that is closed under $\kappa$-filtered colimits for some $\kappa$.
examples: The $(\infty,1)$-category of spaces ($\infty$-groupoids) and the $(\infty,1)$-category of spectra are presentable.
For every small $(\infty,1)$-category $D$, the presheaf $(\infty,1)$-category on $D$ is presentable.
Non-example: the $(\infty,1)$-category of finite spaces has no infinite coproducts, so it lacks small colimits and is not presentable.

steps: Let $C$ be a [locally presentable category](c:locally-presentable-category) and take its nerve $N(C)$, an $(\infty,1)$-category with discrete mapping spaces.
A colimit in $N(C)$ of a diagram $K\to N(C)$ is a colimit in $C$ over the homotopy category of $K$, so $N(C)$ has small colimits.
The $\kappa$-compact generators of $C$ stay $\kappa$-compact in $N(C)$ and generate it under $\kappa$-filtered colimits.
So $N(C)$ is a presentable $(\infty,1)$-category, and the general notion also allows non-discrete mapping spaces.
links.why: It shows that presentable $(\infty,1)$-categories extend the classical locally presentable categories to higher mapping spaces.

reminder: A primitive element $x$ of a [bialgebra](c:bialgebra) satisfies $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$.
definition: In a [bialgebra](c:bialgebra) $H$ over a field with comultiplication $\Delta$, an element $x$ is primitive when $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$ in the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $H\otimes H$. The primitive elements form a Lie subalgebra of $H$ under the commutator $[x,y]=xy-yx$.
examples: In the polynomial algebra $k[x]$ with $\Delta(x)=x\otimes1+1\otimes x$, the generator $x$ is primitive.
In the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ of a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak{g}$, every element of $\mathfrak{g}$ is primitive.
Non-example: in $k[x]$ the element $x^2$ is not primitive, because $\Delta(x^2)=x^2\otimes1+2\,x\otimes x+1\otimes x^2$.
Non-example: a group element $g$ in a group algebra has $\Delta(g)=g\otimes g$, so it is group-like and not primitive.

reminder: The principal curvatures at a point of a surface are the largest and smallest normal curvatures there.
definition: At a point $p$ of a [surface](c:surface) in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with a chosen unit normal, the normal curvature $\kappa(v)$ in the unit tangent direction $v$ is the curvature of the plane curve cut out by the plane through $p$ that contains $v$ and the normal. The principal curvatures $\kappa_1\ge\kappa_2$ are the maximum and the minimum of $\kappa(v)$ over all unit vectors $v$. They are the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) of the shape operator, which represents the [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form), and reversing the normal changes their signs.
examples: A sphere of radius $r$ has both principal curvatures equal to $1/r$ at every point, for the inward normal.
A cylinder of radius $r$ has the principal curvatures $1/r$ and $0$.
The saddle $z=xy$ has the principal curvatures $1$ and $-1$ at the origin.
Non-example: the Gaussian curvature $\kappa_1\kappa_2$ and the mean curvature $(\kappa_1+\kappa_2)/2$ are combinations of the principal curvatures, but they are not principal curvatures.

reminder: A principal [ideal](c:ideal) is an ideal that one element generates.
definition: In a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the principal ideal that $a\in R$ generates is $(a)=aR=\{ar:r\in R\}$, the smallest [ideal](c:ideal) of $R$ that contains $a$. In a non-commutative ring, the left principal ideal of $a$ is $Ra$.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}$ the ideal $(6)=\{6k:k\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is principal, and in fact every ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is principal.
In $K[x]$, for a field $K$, the ideal $(x^2-1)$ is principal.
Non-example: the ideal $(2,x)$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not principal. A single generator would divide both $2$ and $x$, so it would be $\pm1$, but $(2,x)$ is not the whole ring.

steps: Start with an element $a$ of a commutative ring $R$.
The set $aR$ is closed under addition and under multiplication by elements of $R$, so it is an [ideal](c:ideal).
It contains $a$, and every ideal that contains $a$ contains $aR$.
So a principal ideal is an ideal with one generator, while a general ideal may need many generators.
links.why: It shows that a principal ideal is an ideal with a single generator.

reminder: The principal symbol of a differential operator keeps only its terms of highest order and replaces derivatives by covector variables.
definition: For a [differential operator](c:differential-operator) $P=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}a_\alpha(x)\partial^\alpha$ of order $m$, the principal symbol is the function $\sigma_m(P)(x,\xi)=\sum_{|\alpha|=m}a_\alpha(x)\xi^\alpha$ on the [cotangent bundle](c:cotangent-bundle), where some authors add a factor $i^m$. It is the highest-degree homogeneous part of the full [symbol](c:symbol-of-a-differential-operator), and the same idea gives the leading homogeneous term of a [pseudodifferential operator](c:pseudodifferential-operator).
examples: The Laplacian $\partial_x^2+\partial_y^2$ has the principal symbol $\xi^2+\eta^2=|\xi|^2$.
For $P=a(x)\partial_x^2+b(x)\partial_x+c(x)$ the principal symbol is $a(x)\xi^2$, and the terms with $b$ and $c$ do not appear.
The heat operator $\partial_t-\Delta$ has order $2$ and the principal symbol $-|\xi|^2$, because $\partial_t$ has order $1$.
Non-example: the full symbol $a(x)\xi^2+b(x)\xi+c(x)$ is not the principal symbol, because it keeps the lower-order terms.

reminder: A probability measure is non-negative, has total mass $1$, and is countably additive on disjoint events.
definition: The probability axioms of Kolmogorov say that a function $P$ on a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of a sample space $\Omega$ is a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) when $P(A)\ge0$ for every event $A\in\mathcal{F}$, $P(\Omega)=1$, and $P(\bigcup_iA_i)=\sum_iP(A_i)$ for every countable family of pairwise disjoint events $A_i$.
examples: For a fair die, $\Omega=\{1,\dots,6\}$ and $P(A)=|A|/6$ satisfy all three axioms.
The uniform distribution on $[0,1]$, with $P(A)$ equal to the length of $A$ for Borel sets $A$, satisfies the axioms.
Non-example: assigning $P(\mathrm{heads})=P(\mathrm{tails})=0.7$ to a coin violates the axioms, because additivity then gives $P(\Omega)=1.4\neq1$.

steps: Start with a function $P$ that satisfies the probability axioms on a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra).
It is non-negative and countably additive, and taking every $A_i=\varnothing$ forces $P(\varnothing)=0$.
So $P$ is a [measure](c:measure) on the measurable space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$.
The special case adds the normalization $P(\Omega)=1$.
links.why: It shows that measure theory applies to probability, which is a measure of total mass $1$.

reminder: In the product order, $(a,b)\le(a',b')$ holds exactly when $a\le a'$ and $b\le b'$.
definition: Let $(A,\le)$ and $(B,\le)$ be [partially ordered sets](c:partial-order). The product order on the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $A\times B$ is given by $(a,b)\le(a',b')$ when $a\le a'$ in $A$ and $b\le b'$ in $B$. It is a partial order, and the same rule defines it on any finite product, such as $\mathbb{N}^n$ or $\mathbb{R}^n$.
examples: In $\mathbb{N}^2$ one has $(1,3)\le(2,3)$, but $(1,3)$ and $(2,1)$ are incomparable.
On $\{0,1\}^n$ the product order is the inclusion order of the subsets of an $n$-element set.
Non-example: the lexicographic order on $\mathbb{N}^2$ is a different order. There $(1,5)<(2,0)$, but this fails in the product order.

reminder: A production function gives the greatest output that a firm can make from each bundle of inputs.
definition: A production function is a [function](c:function) $f:\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^n\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ that gives, for each bundle $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ of inputs such as capital and labour, the largest output $f(x)$ that a firm can produce from $x$. It is usually assumed to be [monotone](c:monotone-function) in each input, with $f(0)=0$.
examples: The Cobb-Douglas function $f(K,L)=AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}$, with $A>0$ and $0<\alpha<1$, is a production function.
The Leontief function $f(K,L)=\min(K/a,L/b)$ models inputs that must be used in fixed proportions.
The linear function $f(K,L)=aK+bL$ models inputs that are perfect substitutes.
Non-example: a cost function $C(w,y)$ gives the least cost of the output $y$ at the input prices $w$, so it is not a production function, which maps inputs to output.

reminder: A projective involution is a [projective transformation](c:projective-transformation) that is its own inverse.
definition: A projective involution is a [projective transformation](c:projective-transformation) $\sigma$ of a [projective space](c:projective-space) with $\sigma\circ\sigma=\mathrm{id}$. It comes from an invertible linear map $T$ with $T^2=\lambda\cdot\mathrm{id}$ for some scalar $\lambda\neq0$, and some authors exclude the identity map.
examples: On the projective line, the map $z\mapsto-z$ is an involution with the two fixed points $0$ and $\infty$.
The map $z\mapsto-1/z$ is an involution of the real projective line with no real fixed point, and its fixed points over $\mathbb{C}$ are $\pm i$.
Non-example: the translation $z\mapsto z+1$ is a projective transformation, but applying it twice gives $z\mapsto z+2$, so it is not an involution.

steps: The projective transformations of a projective space form a group, the projective linear group.
A projective involution is an element $\sigma$ of this group with $\sigma^2=1$.
An element of a group that squares to the identity is an [involution](c:involution).
So a projective involution is an involution of the projective space that is also a projective transformation.
links.why: It shows that results about involutions, such as the split into fixed points and swapped pairs, apply to projective involutions.

reminder: A projective line is the set of lines through the origin of a two-dimensional vector space.
definition: The projective line over a field $K$ is the [projective space](c:projective-space) of dimension $1$, $\mathbb{P}^1(K)=(K^2\setminus\{0\})/K^\times$, whose points $[x:y]$ are the one-dimensional subspaces of $K^2$. It is the affine line $K$ together with one point at infinity, where $[x:1]$ corresponds to $x$ and $[1:0]$ is $\infty$.
examples: The real projective line $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{R})$ is a circle, and $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ is the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere).
Over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ the projective line has $q+1$ points.
Non-example: the affine line $K$ is not a projective line, because it lacks the point at infinity.

steps: Take the [projective space](c:projective-space) $\mathbb{P}(V)$ of a vector space $V$ over $K$, whose points are the lines through $0$ in $V$.
Its dimension is $\dim V-1$.
Require this dimension to be $1$, so that $V\cong K^2$.
Then $\mathbb{P}(V)$ is a projective line.
links.why: It shows that a projective line is a projective space of dimension one, so general results apply to it.

steps: Start with the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1(K)$ over a field $K$.
Take $K=\mathbb{C}$, so $\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})=\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$.
The coordinate $[x:y]\mapsto x/y$ gives it the structure of a complex manifold.
This complex manifold is the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere).
links.why: It shows that the Riemann sphere is the projective line over the complex numbers.

reminder: A proof system is a set of axioms and rules that tells which formulas count as proved.
definition: A proof system for a formal language consists of [axioms](c:axiom) and inference rules that define which finite derivations count as proofs. A [formula](c:formula) is provable when some derivation ends with it. Common styles are the [Hilbert system](c:hilbert-system), [natural deduction](c:natural-deduction) and the [sequent calculus](c:sequent-calculus).
examples: A Hilbert system for propositional logic has axiom schemes for implication and negation, and the single rule [modus ponens](c:modus-ponens).
Natural deduction has introduction and elimination rules for each connective.
Non-example: a bare list of axioms with no rule for deriving new formulas is not a proof system, because it gives no derivations.

reminder: A proper action is a continuous group action for which the map $(g,x)\mapsto(x,gx)$ is proper.
definition: A continuous [action](c:group-action) of a [topological group](c:topological-group) $G$ on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is proper when the map $G\times X\to X\times X$, $(g,x)\mapsto(x,gx)$, is a [proper map](c:proper-map), that is, closed with compact fibres. For a locally compact Hausdorff space $X$ this means that the preimage of every compact set is compact, so the action behaves like the action of a compact group.
examples: Every continuous action of a [compact group](c:compact-group) is proper.
For compact $K,L\subset\mathbb{R}$ only finitely many integers $n$ satisfy $(n+K)\cap L\neq\varnothing$, so translation by $\mathbb{Z}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is proper.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on the circle by an irrational rotation is not proper, because the preimage of the compact set $S^1\times S^1$ is $\mathbb{Z}\times S^1$, which is not compact.

steps: Start with a proper action of a topological group $G$ on a Hausdorff space $X$.
Add the condition that $G$ is discrete.
For compact sets $K,L$, the preimage of $K\times L$ is a union of the compact pieces $\{g\}\times(K\cap g^{-1}L)$.
This preimage is compact exactly when only finitely many $g$ satisfy $gK\cap L\neq\varnothing$, which is [proper discontinuity](c:properly-discontinuous-action).
links.why: It shows that proper actions extend properly discontinuous actions from discrete groups to all topological groups.

reminder: A proper birational map is a proper morphism that is an isomorphism over a dense open subset.
definition: A proper birational map is a [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ that is [proper](c:is-proper) and [birational](c:birational-morphism): there is a dense open set $V\subseteq Y$ such that $f^{-1}(V)$ is dense in $X$ and $f^{-1}(V)\to V$ is an isomorphism. It is the standard form of a modification, such as a blow-up or a resolution of singularities.
examples: The blow-up of a smooth surface at a point is proper and birational, and it replaces the point by a projective line.
A resolution of singularities $\tilde X\to X$ is a proper birational morphism.
The normalization of the nodal cubic $y^2=x^2(x+1)$ is finite, so it is proper, and it is birational.
Non-example: the open inclusion $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^1$ is birational but not proper, because its image is not closed.

steps: Start with a [birational morphism](c:birational-morphism) $f:X\to Y$, which is an isomorphism over a dense open set $V\subseteq Y$.
Add the condition that $f$ is proper.
A proper morphism is closed, so its image is closed, and the image contains the dense set $V$.
So $f$ is surjective, and a proper birational map is a birational morphism that is also surjective and proper.
links.why: It shows that properness forces a birational morphism to be surjective.

steps: Start with a [proper morphism](c:is-proper) $f:X\to Y$, which is separated, universally closed and of finite type.
Add the condition that $f$ is an isomorphism over a dense open set $V\subseteq Y$ with $f^{-1}(V)$ dense in $X$.
Then $f$ changes $Y$ only over the closed complement of $V$.
So $f$ is a proper birational map, a modification of $Y$.
links.why: It shows that a proper birational map is a proper morphism that differs from an isomorphism only over a small closed set.

reminder: A proper convex function is convex, never takes the value $-\infty$, and is finite at some point.
definition: A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is a proper [convex function](c:convex-function) when $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)$ for $0\le\lambda\le1$, and its effective domain $\mathrm{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}$ is not empty. Here the values lie in the [extended real numbers](c:extended-real-number), and the value $-\infty$ is excluded.
examples: The functions $f(x)=x^2$ and $f(x)=|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$ are proper convex functions.
The indicator function of a non-empty [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$, equal to $0$ on $C$ and $+\infty$ outside, is a proper convex function.
Non-example: the constant functions $+\infty$ and $-\infty$ are convex in the extended sense, but neither is proper.

steps: Take a [convex function](c:convex-function) $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$.
Its effective domain $\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set), possibly empty.
Add the conditions that this domain is not empty and that $f$ never takes the value $-\infty$.
Then $f$ is a proper convex function.
links.why: It shows that properness only removes the degenerate extended-valued convex functions.

reminder: In a properly discontinuous action, only finitely many group elements move one compact set to meet another.
definition: An action of a group $\Gamma$ by homeomorphisms on a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is properly discontinuous when, for all compact sets $K,L\subseteq X$, only finitely many $\gamma\in\Gamma$ satisfy $\gamma K\cap L\neq\varnothing$. Some authors require only that each point has a neighbourhood $U$ with $\gamma U\cap U\neq\varnothing$ for finitely many $\gamma$; for a free action on a Hausdorff space this makes the quotient map a [covering space](c:covering-space) projection.
examples: The group $\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $\mathbb{R}$ by $n\cdot x=x+n$ in a properly discontinuous way, and the quotient is the circle.
The group $\mathbb{Z}^2$ acts on $\mathbb{R}^2$ by translations in a properly discontinuous way, and the quotient is the torus.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ acting on the circle by an irrational rotation is not properly discontinuous, because for $K=L=S^1$ every $n$ gives $nK\cap L\neq\varnothing$.

steps: Let $\Gamma$ be a discrete group acting properly discontinuously on a Hausdorff space $X$.
For compact sets $K,L$, the preimage of $K\times L$ under $(\gamma,x)\mapsto(x,\gamma x)$ is a union of the pieces $\{\gamma\}\times(K\cap\gamma^{-1}L)$.
Each piece is compact, and only finitely many are non-empty, so the preimage is compact.
Hence the action is a [proper action](c:proper-action), and the discrete case adds the finiteness of $\{\gamma:\gamma K\cap L\neq\varnothing\}$.
links.why: It shows that results about proper actions, such as Hausdorff quotients, hold for properly discontinuous actions.

reminder: Propositional logic studies formulas built from atomic propositions with connectives and no quantifiers.
definition: Propositional logic is the logic of [formulas](c:formula) built from atomic [propositions](c:proposition) $p,q,\dots$ with the [logical connectives](c:logical-connective) $\neg,\wedge,\vee,\to$, and it has no variables to quantify. A truth assignment gives each atom a [truth value](c:truth-value) and so fixes the truth value of every formula. A formula that is true under every assignment is a [tautology](c:tautology).
examples: The formulas $(p\wedge q)\to p$ and $p\vee\neg p$ are tautologies of classical propositional logic.
The formula $p\to q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false.
Non-example: $\forall x\,P(x)\to P(a)$ is a formula of first-order logic, not of propositional logic, because it uses a quantifier and a variable.

steps: Treat each atomic proposition $p$ as a predicate symbol with no arguments.
A propositional formula is then a first-order formula with no variables and no quantifiers.
A truth assignment is a first-order structure that gives each of these symbols a truth value.
So every propositional tautology is a valid formula of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic).
links.why: It shows that propositional logic is the quantifier-free core of first-order logic, so its results carry over.

reminder: A pseudorandom measure is a non-negative weight on $\mathbb{Z}_N$ with mean near $1$ and nearly uniform counts of linear patterns.
definition:
A pseudorandom measure is a function $
u:\mathbb{Z}_N	o[0,\infty)$ with [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mathbb{E}\,
u=1+o(1)$ that satisfies the linear forms condition and the correlation condition of Green and Tao. The linear forms condition says that $\mathbb{E}\prod_j
u(\psi_j(x))=1+o(1)$ for bounded systems of linear forms $\psi_j$ over [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic), so $
u$ counts patterns like the constant $1$; the correlation condition bounds averages of products $
u(x+h_1)\cdots
u(x+h_m)$ by sums of weights with bounded moments.
examples: The constant function $\nu\equiv1$ is pseudorandom.
A suitably normalised majorant of the primes, built from truncated divisor sums, is the pseudorandom measure used to prove the Green-Tao theorem.
Non-example: the normalised indicator of the primes is not pseudorandom, because it vanishes on even numbers, so $\mathbb{E}\,\nu(x)\nu(x+1)$ is far from $1$.

reminder: A quadratic residue modulo $n$ is a number coprime to $n$ that is congruent to a square modulo $n$.
definition: An integer $a$ is a quadratic residue modulo $n$ when $a$ is coprime to $n$ and the congruence $x^2\equiv a\pmod n$ has a solution $x$ in the [integers](c:integer), using [modular arithmetic](c:modular-arithmetic). If $a$ is coprime to $n$ and there is no solution, then $a$ is a quadratic non-residue.
examples: Modulo $7$ the squares of $1,\dots,6$ are $1,4,2,2,4,1$, so the quadratic residues are $1$, $2$ and $4$.
Modulo an odd prime $p$, exactly $(p-1)/2$ of the non-zero classes are quadratic residues.
Non-example: $3$ is a quadratic non-residue modulo $7$, because no square is congruent to $3$ modulo $7$.

reminder: A quadrilateral is a [polygon](c:polygon) with four sides and four vertices.
definition: A quadrilateral $ABCD$ is a closed [polygon](c:polygon) with the four vertices $A,B,C,D$ and the four sides $AB,BC,CD,DA$. In the usual sense, a simple quadrilateral, the sides meet only at shared endpoints, and the interior angles add up to $360^\circ$.
examples: Squares, rectangles, rhombi, parallelograms and trapezoids are convex quadrilaterals.
A dart, which has one reflex angle, is a non-convex quadrilateral.
Non-example: a bow-tie, whose two opposite sides cross, is not a simple quadrilateral.

steps: A [polygon](c:polygon) is a closed chain of $n\ge3$ line segments joined end to end.
Fix the number of segments to be $n=4$.
Then the polygon has four vertices and four sides, and it is a quadrilateral.
links.why: It shows that every fact about polygons holds for quadrilaterals, with $n=4$.

steps: Start with a quadrilateral $ABCD$.
Add the condition that $AB\parallel CD$ and $BC\parallel DA$.
Then both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, and $ABCD$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram).
links.why: It shows that a parallelogram is a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides.

steps: Start with a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$.
Add the condition that all four vertices lie on one circle.
Then $ABCD$ is a [cyclic quadrilateral](c:cyclic-quadrilateral), and its opposite angles add up to $180^\circ$.
links.why: It shows that a cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.

reminder: A quasi-category is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) in which every inner [horn](c:horn) has a filler.
definition: A quasi-category is a [simplicial set](c:simplicial-set) $X$ such that, for $n\ge2$ and $0<k<n$, every map from the inner [horn](c:horn) $\Lambda^n_k\to X$ extends to a map $\Delta^n\to X$. It models an [(infinity,1)-category](c:infinity-1-category): vertices are objects, edges are morphisms, and a $2$-simplex witnesses a composite of two edges.
examples: The [nerve](c:nerve) of a small category is a quasi-category, and its fillers are unique.
Every [Kan complex](c:kan-complex) is a quasi-category, because it has fillers for all horns, inner or outer.
Non-example: the horn $\Lambda^2_1$ itself, two edges $0\to1\to2$ with no edge $0\to2$, is not a quasi-category, because its identity map has no filler.

steps: Start with a quasi-category $X$, which has fillers for all inner horns $\Lambda^n_k$ with $0<k<n$.
Add the condition that $X$ also has fillers for the outer horns, where $k=0$ or $k=n$.
Then $X$ is a [Kan complex](c:kan-complex).
In a Kan complex every edge is invertible up to homotopy, so it models an $\infty$-groupoid.
links.why: It shows that Kan complexes are the quasi-categories in which all morphisms are invertible.

steps: Start with a quasi-category $X$.
Add the condition that every inner horn has a unique filler.
Then $X$ is isomorphic to the [nerve](c:nerve) of a category, namely its homotopy category.
So ordinary categories are exactly the quasi-categories with unique inner fillers.
links.why: It shows that quasi-categories extend ordinary categories by allowing non-unique composites.

reminder: A function is quasi-convex when every sublevel set is [convex](c:convex-set).
definition: A function $f:C\to\mathbb{R}$ on a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$ is quasi-convex when each sublevel set $\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}$ is convex. Equivalently, $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $0\le\lambda\le1$.
examples: Every [convex function](c:convex-function) is quasi-convex, for example $f(x)=x^2$.
Every monotone function on $\mathbb{R}$ is quasi-convex, for example $f(x)=x^3$, because its sublevel sets are intervals.
Non-example: $f(x)=-x^2$ is not quasi-convex, because $\{x:f(x)\le-1\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)$ is not convex.

steps: Let $f$ be a [convex function](c:convex-function), so $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)$.
The right side is a weighted average of $f(x)$ and $f(y)$, so it is at most $\max\{f(x),f(y)\}$.
So $f$ satisfies the quasi-convex inequality.
The convex case adds the stronger weighted-average bound.
links.why: It shows that convexity of the function implies convexity of all its sublevel sets.

reminder: A quasi-finite morphism is of finite type and has only finitely many points in each fibre.
definition: A [morphism of schemes](c:morphism-of-schemes) $f:X\to Y$ is quasi-finite when it is quasi-compact and [locally of finite type](c:locally-of-finite-type), and every [fibre](c:fiber) $f^{-1}(y)$ is a finite set of points. It need not be proper, so it is weaker than finite.
examples: Every [finite morphism](c:is-finite), such as $\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{C}[x]\to\mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{C}[x^2]$, is quasi-finite.
The open immersion $\mathbb{A}^1\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbb{A}^1$ is quasi-finite, although it is not proper.
Non-example: the structure map $\mathbb{A}^1_k\to\mathrm{Spec}\,k$ has the fibre $\mathbb{A}^1_k$, which has infinitely many points, so it is not quasi-finite.

steps: Start with a quasi-finite morphism $f:X\to Y$.
Add the condition that $f$ is proper.
A proper quasi-finite morphism is a [finite morphism](c:is-finite).
Conversely every finite morphism is quasi-finite, so properness is the only extra condition.
links.why: It shows that finite morphisms are the proper quasi-finite morphisms.

steps: Start with an [étale morphism](c:etale) $f:X\to Y$ of finite type.
An étale morphism is unramified, so each fibre is a disjoint union of spectra of finite separable field extensions.
So every fibre is a finite set of points, and $f$ is quasi-finite.
The étale case adds flatness and unramifiedness.
links.why: It shows that every étale morphism of finite type is quasi-finite.

reminder: A quasi-isometry preserves distances up to fixed multiplicative and additive errors, and its image comes within a fixed distance of every point.
definition: A map $f:X\to Y$ between [metric spaces](c:metric-space) is a quasi-isometry when there are constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $C\ge0$ such that $\frac1\lambda d(x,x')-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(x'))\le\lambda d(x,x')+\varepsilon$ for all $x,x'\in X$, and every point of $Y$ lies within distance $C$ of $f(X)$. Then $X$ and $Y$ are quasi-isometric, which is an equivalence relation, and $f$ need not be continuous.
examples: The inclusion $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{R}$ is a quasi-isometry, because it preserves distances and every real number is within $1/2$ of an integer.
A finite-index subgroup of a finitely generated group is quasi-isometric to the group, when both carry word metrics.
Every bounded metric space is quasi-isometric to a point.
Non-example: the inclusion $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^2$, $x\mapsto(x,0)$, is not a quasi-isometry, because points far from the horizontal axis are at unbounded distance from its image.

steps: Start with a quasi-isometry $f:X\to Y$ with constants $\lambda$, $\varepsilon$ and $C$.
Add the conditions $\lambda=1$, $\varepsilon=0$ and $C=0$.
Then $d(f(x),f(x'))=d(x,x')$ for all $x,x'$, and $f$ is surjective.
So $f$ is a bijective [isometry](c:isometry-equiv).
links.why: It shows that a quasi-isometry is a bijective isometry with the errors allowed to be non-zero.

reminder: A quaternion algebra over a field is a four-dimensional algebra with basis $1,i,j,k$, where $i^2=a$, $j^2=b$ and $ij=-ji=k$.
definition: For a [field](c:field) $F$ of characteristic not $2$ and $a,b\in F^\times$, the quaternion algebra $(a,b)_F$ is the four-dimensional [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) over $F$ with basis $1,i,j,k$ and the rules $i^2=a$, $j^2=b$ and $k=ij=-ji$. It is a central simple algebra, so it is either a division algebra or isomorphic to the matrix algebra $M_2(F)$. Over a commutative ring one can use the more general rules $i^2=c_1+c_2i$ and $j^2=c_3$.
examples: Hamilton's [quaternions](c:quaternion) are the algebra $(-1,-1)_{\mathbb{R}}$, which is a division algebra.
The algebra $(1,1)_{\mathbb{R}}$ is isomorphic to $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, with $i=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ and $j=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}$ has dimension $2$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and $M_3(\mathbb{R})$ has dimension $9$, so neither is a quaternion algebra over $\mathbb{R}$.

steps: Start with a quaternion algebra $(a,b)_F$ over a field $F$.
Take $F=\mathbb{R}$ and $a=b=-1$.
Then $i^2=j^2=-1$ and $ij=-ji=k$, which are the rules of the [quaternions](c:quaternion).
So Hamilton's quaternions are the algebra $(-1,-1)_{\mathbb{R}}$.
links.why: It shows that Hamilton's quaternions are one quaternion algebra among many, one for each choice of field and parameters.

reminder: A Quillen adjunction is an adjunction between [model categories](c:model-category) whose left adjoint preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations.
definition: A Quillen adjunction is an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) $F\dashv G$ between [model categories](c:model-category) in which the left adjoint $F$ preserves [cofibrations](c:cofibration) and trivial cofibrations. Equivalently, the right adjoint $G$ preserves [fibrations](c:fibration) and trivial fibrations.
examples: Geometric realization and the singular complex form a Quillen adjunction $|\cdot|\dashv\mathrm{Sing}$ between simplicial sets and topological spaces, and it is even a Quillen equivalence.
The free abelian group functor from simplicial sets to simplicial abelian groups, left adjoint to the forgetful functor, is a Quillen adjunction.

Non-example: the identity functor from simplicial sets with the Kan-Quillen structure to simplicial sets with the Joyal structure is not a left Quillen functor, because $\{0\}\to\Delta^1$ is a trivial cofibration for Kan-Quillen but not for Joyal.

steps: A Quillen adjunction is an [adjunction](c:adjoint-functor) $F\dashv G$ between the underlying categories of two model categories.
Add the condition that $F$ preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations.
This condition is equivalent to $G$ preserving fibrations and trivial fibrations.
So the adjunction passes to a derived adjunction between the homotopy categories.
links.why: It shows that a Quillen adjunction is an adjunction that respects the homotopy theory of both sides.

steps: Start with a Quillen adjunction $F\dashv G$.
Add the condition that for cofibrant $A$ and fibrant $X$, a map $FA\to X$ is a weak equivalence exactly when its adjoint $A\to GX$ is.
Equivalently, the derived adjunction is an equivalence of homotopy categories.
Then the pair is a [Quillen equivalence](c:quillen-equivalence).
links.why: It shows that a Quillen equivalence is a Quillen adjunction that induces an equivalence of homotopy theories.

reminder: The ramification index of a prime $\mathfrak P$ over $\mathfrak p$ is the exponent of $\mathfrak P$ in the factorization of $\mathfrak p$.
definition: Let $A$ be a [Dedekind domain](c:dedekind-domain), let $L$ be a finite separable [extension](c:field-extension) of its fraction field, and let $B$ be the integral closure of $A$ in $L$. For a non-zero [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ one has the [prime ideal factorization](c:prime-ideal-factorization) $\mathfrak pB=\prod_i\mathfrak P_i^{e_i}$, and the exponent $e_i=e(\mathfrak P_i|\mathfrak p)$ is the ramification index of $\mathfrak P_i$ over $\mathfrak p$.
examples: In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ one has $(2)=(1+i)^2$, so the prime $(1+i)$ has ramification index $2$ over $2$.
In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ one has $(5)=(2+i)(2-i)$, and both primes have ramification index $1$ over $5$.
Non-example: the residue degree $f=[B/\mathfrak P:A/\mathfrak p]$ is a different number. In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ the prime $(3)$ has $e=1$ and $f=2$.

reminder: The rank of a set is the least ordinal $\alpha$ such that the set is a subset of $V_\alpha$.
definition: In the [cumulative hierarchy](c:cumulative-hierarchy), defined by $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal{P}(V_\alpha)$ and $V_\lambda=\bigcup_{\alpha<\lambda}V_\alpha$ for limit $\lambda$, the rank of a set $x$ is the least [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ with $x\subseteq V_\alpha$. Equivalently, $\mathrm{rank}(x)=\sup\{\mathrm{rank}(y)+1:y\in x\}$, and under the axiom of foundation every set has a rank.
examples: One has $\mathrm{rank}(\varnothing)=0$, $\mathrm{rank}(\{\varnothing\})=1$ and $\mathrm{rank}(\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\})=2$.
The rank of an ordinal $\alpha$ is $\alpha$, so the set $\mathbb{N}$ has rank $\omega$.
Non-example: a set $x$ with $x=\{x\}$ would need $\mathrm{rank}(x)=\mathrm{rank}(x)+1$, so it has no rank, and the axiom of foundation excludes it.

reminder: The rationalization of a nilpotent space $X$ is a map $X\to X_{\mathbb{Q}}$ that tensors every homotopy group with $\mathbb{Q}$.
definition: For a [nilpotent space](c:nilpotent-space) $X$, the rationalization is a map $X\to X_{\mathbb{Q}}$ into a space whose [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) are $\mathbb{Q}$-vector spaces, such that $\pi_n(X)\otimes\mathbb{Q}\to\pi_n(X_{\mathbb{Q}})$ is an isomorphism for all $n\ge1$. For $n=1$ the tensor product means the Malcev completion of the nilpotent group $\pi_1(X)$. The rationalization is unique up to [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence).
examples: The odd spheres have the rationalizations $S^{2n+1}_{\mathbb{Q}}=K(\mathbb{Q},2n+1)$, because $\pi_k(S^{2n+1})\otimes\mathbb{Q}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ for $k=2n+1$ and $0$ otherwise.
An even sphere $S^{2n}$ with $n\ge1$ has a rationalization with $\pi_{2n}\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{Q}$ and $\pi_{4n-1}\otimes\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{Q}$, and no other non-zero rational homotopy groups.
Non-example: the identity map of $S^3$ is not a rationalization, because $\pi_3(S^3)=\mathbb{Z}$ is not a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space.

steps: Take the [localization of a space](c:localization-of-a-space) at a set $P$ of primes, which makes the primes in $P$ invertible on all homotopy groups.
Let $P$ be the set of all primes.
Making every prime invertible tensors each homotopy group with $\mathbb{Q}$.
So the localization at all primes is the rationalization $X_{\mathbb{Q}}$.
links.why: It shows that rationalization is localization with every prime inverted, so localization results apply.

reminder: The ray class group is the group of ideals coprime to a modulus, modulo principal ideals congruent to $1$ modulo it.
definition: For a [number field](c:number-field) $K$ and a modulus $\mathfrak m$ (a non-zero ideal of the [ring of integers](c:ring-of-integers) together with some real places), the ray class group is $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathfrak m}(K)=I^{\mathfrak m}/P_{\mathfrak m}$. Here $I^{\mathfrak m}$ is the group of [fractional ideals](c:fractional-ideal) coprime to $\mathfrak m$, and $P_{\mathfrak m}$ is the subgroup of principal ideals $(\alpha)$ with $\alpha\equiv1$ modulo $\mathfrak m$ and $\alpha$ positive at the real places in $\mathfrak m$.
examples: For $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and the modulus $\mathfrak m=(N)\infty$, the ray class group is $(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})^\times$.
For $K=\mathbb{Q}$ and the modulus $\mathfrak m=(5)$ with no real place, the ray class group has order $2$ and equals $(\mathbb{Z}/5\mathbb{Z})^\times/\{\pm1\}$.

Non-example: the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) of $\mathbb{Q}$ is trivial, but the ray class group of $\mathbb{Q}$ for the modulus $(5)$ has order $2$, so the two groups differ unless the modulus is trivial.

steps: Start with the ray class group $\mathrm{Cl}_{\mathfrak m}(K)$ for a modulus $\mathfrak m$.
Take the trivial modulus $\mathfrak m=1$.
Then every fractional ideal is coprime to $\mathfrak m$, and every principal ideal is allowed.
So $\mathrm{Cl}_1(K)=I/P$ is the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group).
links.why: It shows that the ideal class group is the ray class group for the trivial modulus.

reminder: A real-analytic manifold has an atlas whose transition maps are real-analytic functions.
definition: A real-analytic manifold of dimension $n$ is a [manifold](c:manifold) with an [atlas](c:atlas) of charts into open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$, such that every transition map is a real-[analytic function](c:analytic-function), that is, locally equal to a convergent power series. Each such manifold is also a smooth manifold.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^n$, the spheres $S^n$ and the tori are real-analytic manifolds, and so is every Lie group.
The real projective plane has a real-analytic atlas with transition maps that are quotients of polynomials.
Non-example: the two charts $x$ and $x|x|$ on $\mathbb{R}$ do not form an analytic atlas, because $x|x|$ is not twice differentiable at $0$.

steps: Take a real-analytic manifold with its analytic atlas.
Every real-analytic function is smooth, so all transition maps are smooth.
So the same atlas makes the space a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold).
The analytic case adds that the transition maps are locally given by power series.
links.why: It shows that every result about smooth manifolds holds for real-analytic ones.

reminder: The real projective plane is the space of lines through the origin in three-dimensional real space.
definition: The real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) over the [real numbers](c:real-number): the set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$, or equivalently the sphere $S^2$ with each point identified with its antipode. It is a [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $2$ that has no [orientation](c:orientation-of-a-manifold), and its Euler characteristic is $1$.
examples: A Möbius band with a disc glued along its boundary circle is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{RP}^2$.
The fundamental group of $\mathbb{RP}^2$ is $\mathbb{Z}/2$, because the sphere $S^2$ is its universal double cover.
Non-example: the sphere $S^2$ is orientable and has Euler characteristic $2$, so it is not $\mathbb{RP}^2$.

steps: Take the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) $\mathbb{P}^2(K)$ over a field $K$, the set of lines through $0$ in $K^3$.
Choose the field $K=\mathbb{R}$ of real numbers.
Then $\mathbb{P}^2(\mathbb{R})$ is the set of lines through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^3$, which is $\mathbb{RP}^2$, a closed surface.
links.why: It shows that the real projective plane is the projective plane over the real numbers, with extra topology.

reminder: A set of natural numbers is recursive when an algorithm decides membership in finitely many steps.
definition: A subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ of the [natural numbers](c:natural-number) is recursive when its characteristic function is a total [computable function](c:computable-function). That is, an [algorithm](c:algorithm) halts on every input $n$ and answers whether $n\in S$.
examples: The set of even numbers and the set of prime numbers are recursive.
Every finite set of natural numbers is recursive, and so is the complement of a recursive set.
Non-example: the set $K$ of numbers $e$ for which the $e$-th program halts on input $e$ is recursively enumerable but not recursive, by the unsolvability of the [halting problem](c:halting-problem).

steps: Let $S$ be recursive, so an algorithm decides membership in $S$.
Run the algorithm on $0,1,2,\dots$ in turn, and print each $n$ that it accepts.
This procedure prints exactly the elements of $S$, so $S$ is a [recursively enumerable set](c:recursively-enumerable-set).
The recursive case adds that the complement of $S$ is also recursively enumerable.
links.why: It shows that every recursive set is recursively enumerable, and that the converse needs the complement.
